ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Schistosomiasis is a parasitic infection that can cause chronic liver, intestinal, or urogenital disease. Diagnosis relies on stool/urine eggs and serology, while treatment is praziquantel. Management focuses on parasite clearance and complication prevention.

sections.p: Schistosomiasis is caused by trematode worms of the genus Schistosoma. Transmission occurs when skin contacts contaminated freshwater. Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting eggs in stool or urine, supported by serology when eggs are scarce.

t.b: Detects S. mansoni or S. japonicum eggs; positive means active infection.
Detects S. haematobium eggs; positive indicates urogenital disease.
Positive indicates exposure; useful when eggs are not found.

sections.p: Severity is graded by parasite load and organ involvement. Mild disease shows few eggs and minimal symptoms. Moderate disease has moderate egg counts and organ dysfunction. Severe disease presents with high egg counts, portal hypertension, or bladder carcinoma risk.

The primary cause is contact with freshwater infested by Biomphalaria (S. mansoni), Bulinus (S. haematobium), or Oncomelania (S. japonicum) snails. Secondary factors include HIV, malaria, and malnutrition that worsen outcomes.
Early infection causes a Katayama fever with fever, cough, and eosinophilia. Chronic infection leads to abdominal pain, hepatosplenomegaly, portal hypertension, hematuria, or bladder lesions.
Investigations confirm infection, assess organ damage, and guide treatment. In low-resource settings, microscopy is primary; serology and imaging are adjuncts.

t.b: Elevated transaminases or bilirubin indicate hepatic involvement.
Detects periportal fibrosis or bladder wall thickening.
Assesses renal function if urogenital disease suspected.

sections.p: Complications can be life-threatening: portal hypertension with variceal bleeding, bladder carcinoma, severe anemia, or acute hepatic failure. Red flags include massive hematuria, upper GI bleeding, or sudden liver failure.

First-line therapy is praziquantel, chosen for its broad efficacy and low toxicity. Supportive care includes pain control, iron supplementation, and management of portal hypertension. Alternatives like oxamniquine are reserved for specific species.

t.b: Treats all Schistosoma species; reduces egg output.
Treat secondary bacterial infections if present.

sections.p: After treatment, repeat stool/urine exams after 4–6 weeks to confirm cure. Prevention focuses on avoiding freshwater contact, using protective footwear, and snail control.
Schistosomiasis can mimic other causes of portal hypertension such as viral hepatitis or alcoholic cirrhosis, and hematuria can be mistaken for urinary tract infection.
Egg counts may be falsely low in early infection or after treatment. Serology can remain positive long after cure, leading to overdiagnosis.
b: Low egg counts in early disease

faq.q: What is the most common symptom of chronic schistosomiasis?
faq.a: Abdominal pain and hepatosplenomegaly due to periportal fibrosis.
Yes, praziquantel effectively cures most infections, but reinfection is common without preventive measures.
